# The Architect's Role {#sec-what-architect-owns}

::: {.epigraph}
> *"Everyone designs who devises courses of action aimed at changing existing situations into preferred ones."*
>
>  –   Herbert A. Simon, *The Sciences of the Artificial*, 3rd ed. (1996) [@Simon1996SciencesArtificial, p. 111]
:::

::: {.column-margin}
**Author's Note:** Herbert Simon defined design as charting the course from our present situation to a preferred one. This definition places problem choice, abstraction, boundaries, and product tradeoffs at the core of our technical work. While automation can contribute substantially to this journey, our primary architectural contribution lies in shaping that course into a coherent system, establishing exactly what the evidence supports, and making any residual risk fully transparent.
:::

::: {.callout-crux}
If a capable AI-assisted design system can formulate studies, generate artifacts, search design spaces, run tools, interpret failures, and recommend a design, what core technical work do we as architects still contribute?
:::

Let's grant the strongest premise we have established in this book. We assume a capable AI-assisted system can shoulder substantial workloads – everything from initial study formulation through final technical recommendation. This includes coordinating specialized methodologies, driving verification tools, and managing failure-driven revisions across our most exhaustive design studies. Therefore, nothing in our discussion here relies on clinging to a protected set of tasks that only human engineers can execute.

Our role as architects is not simply to mop up whatever tasks automation fails to absorb. Just as the essential difficulty of software engineering lies in rigorously specifying the system rather than merely representing it [@Brooks1986NoSilverBullet], our fundamental technical contribution lies in framing the problem itself. We choose the right abstractions and delineate the critical system boundaries. We synthesize diverse components and disciplines into a single, cohesive, and feasible design. Crucially, we interpret conflicting results, hunt down missing evidence, and declare exactly which uncertainties remain. Ultimately, we actively shape both the architecture of the system and the very design process we use to build it.

Because organizational assignments vary wildly across projects, one person might wear multiple hats. This variability often tempts us to blur the lines between four distinct pillars of engineering work. First, the *domain specialist* qualifies results within a highly focused discipline and owns any technical waivers or signoffs required in that space. Second, *the architect* – whether that is a single lead or a distributed architecture team – integrates those isolated results into a unified system vision. Even if our team divides this architectural burden, we must rigorously define the scope of every technical judgment, explicitly mandate required concurrences, map out escalation paths, and unambiguously assign responsibility for end-to-end system integration.

Third, the *commitment authority* is the specific role or committee authorized to decide whether our proposed design actually advances to the next phase. Whenever we separate architectural vision from product authority, we must ensure that all required product concurrences are formally recorded. Finally, the *accountable organization* provisions the resources for our specialists, architects, and commitment authorities. It maintains the escalation paths and fundamentally owns the consequences of the final product. Simply designating a single lead architect does not absolve the broader organization of its inherent accountability.

Within this framework, our distinctive output as architects is a fully supported architecture recommendation. We must explicitly define the design under consideration, document the environmental conditions and empirical evidence that validate it, expose any lingering risks, and establish the exact triggers – new data or changing constraints – that would force us to narrow or entirely reopen our recommendation. Armed with this comprehensive synthesis, our designated commitment authority can then make a fully informed decision on whether the design advances.

Information flows continuously between these four roles in all directions, yet we must keep our technical deliverables and domains of authority sharply distinct. Our domain specialists push qualified results, failed checks, and unresolved assumptions upward for system-level synthesis. In turn, we – as the architects – push reframed questions and demands for more rigorous stress tests back down to the specialists. We retain direct access to the decisive artifacts and root-cause failures, weaving this cross-layer evidence into an airtight technical recommendation. Our commitment authority receives this deliberate recommendation, preventing them from stumbling into a decision by mere implication. Later, as we monitor deployment metrics or detect material changes in our operational environment, we might reopen this technical analysis. Throughout this lifecycle, the accountable organization ensures our roles, resources, escalation paths, and ultimate product outcomes remain tightly coupled (@fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment).

![**Technical synthesis precedes commitment.** Our domain specialists qualify scoped results and checks. We – the architects – frame the problem, choose the proper abstractions and system boundaries, connect the physical and logical layers, interpret disagreements, and declare the residual risk before presenting a supported technical recommendation. A separate commitment authority then advances, holds, or rejects our design. Our accountable organization resources these distinct roles, and any changed operational conditions can trigger us to reopen the technical work.](images/F11-architecture-synthesis-commitment){#fig-architecture-synthesis-commitment width="100%" fig-alt="An accountable organization surrounds three distinct roles. Domain specialists qualify scoped results, checks, artifacts, and failures. We, the architects, frame the problem, choose our abstractions and system boundaries, connect layers, interpret disagreements, state residual risk, and retain access to decisive artifacts and failures. Our supported technical recommendation then reaches a separate commitment authority that advances, holds, or rejects the design. Continuous monitoring and changed conditions return to the architect and may reopen specialist work."}

This operational separation is never just a rigid, one-way approval chain. A single failed verification check might force us to fundamentally reframe the architecture problem or demand entirely new observational data. Furthermore, late-stage shifts in target workloads, software stacks, EDA tools, manufacturing processes, or deployed environments can completely invalidate our recommendation's foundational assumptions. Crucially, a management commitment decision never rewrites or overrides the hard technical results that preceded it. The remainder of this chapter unpacks our core architectural responsibilities. @tbl-architect-technical-judgments outlines the recurring, high-stakes judgments we make to forge isolated specialist results into one coherent, battle-tested product recommendation.

We can look to NASA's systems-engineering guidance as an established, rigorous precedent for this structural separation. Their decision-analysis framework explicitly produces analytical comparisons and formal recommendations for a distinct decision-making authority. That decision authority is the singular role empowered to execute consequential program choices [@NASA2017SystemsEngineeringHandbook, sec. 6.8 and app. B]. This robust precedent validates our strict distinction between raw technical analysis and authorized product decisions, even if it doesn't rigidly dictate the exact org chart we use to ship a modern silicon project.

We know all too well that every individual IP block or subsystem can operate flawlessly in isolation, yet completely fail to yield a functioning, coherent product when integrated. A deep learning model might perfectly optimize a network link against its local objective function; a compiler backend might successfully validate its lowering path; a formal verifier might cleanly return a counterexample; and our physical-design flows might hit every setup and hold timing margin. As architects, it is entirely our responsibility to step back and verify whether these disparate, specialized victories actually describe a single viable product operating under one globally consistent set of workload, software, interface, memory, power, packaging, and business assumptions.

On their own, these locally qualified victories are completely insufficient to support a high-stakes system recommendation. We must first step in to accurately frame the macroscopic problem, aggressively choose the right abstractions and component boundaries, integrate the stack across physical and logical layers, and ruthlessly arbitrate any disciplinary disagreements. This synthesis produces our ultimate technical recommendation, carefully insulating the raw specialist data from the overarching program claims and the final business decision to advance. The precision and scope of our supporting evidence establish hard limits on what we can ethically present for commitment, and dictate exactly which future disruptions will mandate a full reopening of our technical review.

::: {.callout-learning-objectives}
After reading this chapter, we will be able to:

- Distinguish our architecture recommendations from specialist results, program claims, and organizational commitments.
- Frame coherent architecture problems that maintain integrity across diverse workloads, system boundaries, and AI-assisted interventions.
- Select abstractions, IP components, and verification checks tailored precisely to our technical problem, rather than blindly relying on whatever automation happens to be available.
- Integrate fragmented, cross-disciplinary specialist results into a unified, silicon-ready system design.
- Interpret conflicting evidence, confidently state our bounded recommendations, and identify the exact triggers that mandate a renewed technical review.
:::
## Delegating Work Without Losing Technical Contact

As computer architects, four fundamental conditions govern how we assign design work: we must be able to observe the candidate state, reverse a proposed change, reject a bad result through independent checks, and bound the cross-layer consequences. For example, a bounded array-mapping sweep or a focused tool run often satisfies these conditions, allowing us to confidently hand off the work to a method or domain specialist. However, freezing a software-facing interface presents an entirely different challenge. This constitutes a difficult-to-reverse cross-layer decision that permanently hardens assumptions across compiler and runtime behavior, memory hierarchies, RTL, physical implementation, and ultimate product integration. In such cases, we – as the qualified architecture team – must meticulously reconcile that evidence, empowering the commitment authority to decide whether the transition proceeds. Crucially, both scenarios demand that our team remains competent enough to challenge underlying assumptions and trace failures well beyond the delegated boundary.

Crucially, this assignment rule does not rigidly reserve tasks for human engineers, nor does it attempt to predict which jobs emerging automation might eventually absorb. Instead, it ensures our core architecture judgments remain intimately connected as work flows fluidly between people and tools. As architects, we formulate the overarching system question; we carefully choose our representations alongside their acceptable omissions; we select the right methods and environments; we mandate independent checks; we integrate cross-layer results; and, ultimately, we determine exactly what our combined engineering efforts can safely support.

These continuous judgments must remain a central part of our engineering practice because a robust computer architecture is never simply the union of locally successful component outputs. Rather, it represents a deliberate choice of mechanisms and interfaces designed to work harmoniously under the precise conditions our final product will encounter in the real world. We must actively inspect disagreements, ferret out exceptions, and probe the limits of our models, before definitively determining which residual uncertainties our next design transition can safely carry forward.

This fundamental premise inherently changes how we maintain technical contact with our designs. When we look at previous historical shifts in abstraction – from the advent of logic synthesis [@DeMicheli1994SynthesisOptimization] to the adoption of modern hardware construction languages [@Izraelevitz2017Chisel] – we see that our discipline successfully delegated lower-level tasks precisely because we preserved our technical contact through new diagnostic capabilities. Today, AI-assisted design faces the exact same stringent requirement. While we no longer need to perform every routine task manually, we must stubbornly retain our ability to challenge a formulation, directly inspect decisive artifacts and failures, trace results across complex interfaces, and instantly recognize when a model or check is being pushed outside its established support. If we fail to do so, our delegation will slowly erode the very competence we need to accurately judge the designs we produce.

We can draw a valuable parallel from human-factors research, which clearly distinguishes misuse, when people rely on automation inappropriately, from disuse, when they neglect its capabilities entirely [@ParasuramanRiley1997HumansAutomation]. This critical distinction helps explain exactly why our direct technical contact must survive any level of task delegation. However, it does not unilaterally dictate which specific architecture decisions a human expert or an automated system should ultimately control.

As more of our local work becomes readily delegable, our technical role naturally shifts upstream toward choosing the right problems and abstractions, across the system toward defining rigorous interfaces and checks, and downstream toward accurately interpreting uncertainty and formulating sound recommendations. Importantly, this profound shift does not magically lift us above the gritty engineering details. We must deliberately retain enough hands-on contact with our artifacts, our tools, and our system's failure modes to decisively intervene the moment an abstraction inevitably breaks, or whenever the empirical evidence no longer supports our design decisions.
## Framing the Architecture Problem

We do not just wait for a search to finish before stepping in. As architects, our work begins long before the candidate set even exists, and we remain deeply involved long after a local result looks clean. Our core technical contribution lies in deciding what the system actually is, which cross-layer relationships matter most, and which consequences our studies must expose. We also create or refine the mechanisms, interfaces, abstractions, and fallback options that bind specialist results into a single, coherent system. For example, recognizing that advances in compiler technology shifted the hardware-software boundary is exactly what enabled the RISC approach [@PattersonDitzel1980RISC]. While AI may augment our process, the fundamental architecture question never changes: do all these disparate pieces form a feasible system that meets our product obligations?

Beyond defining the system itself, we must also design the AI-assisted workflows that drive these decisions. We determine which generative methods propose changes, which modeling tools measure relevant properties, which validation checks gate candidates, and which roles resolve disagreements among conflicting results. Ultimately, these methodological choices strictly define what our studies can observe and which architectural conclusions they can support.

Consider the initial Lighthouse prompt – it states a high-level ambition, but an ambition is not yet a well-posed architecture problem. A directive like “Design a low-power, 64-bit RISC-V-based compute subsystem for a real-time mobile XR workload” leaves critical variables entirely open. It ignores the choice of representative workloads, the supported software stack, the product boundary, alternative design points, operating conditions, acceptable tradeoffs, and the specific decisions we need to make. Simply throwing more words at the prompt rarely resolves these fundamental ambiguities. Instead, we must rigorously frame the ambition, transforming it into a challengeable, technical architecture question.

Once we frame the problem, we inherently dictate what our AI-assisted design systems must contain. If we are studying array utilization, our environment might simply need a cycle-level model and a mapping search. However, if we are making a hard decision about freezing that array alongside its software-facing interface, we must expose a much broader reality. We need instruments that capture compiler and runtime behavior, memory traffic, implementation feasibility, total subsystem power, and the cascading consequences of future modifications. It is our architectural question that drives the necessary abstractions and instrumentation, never the other way around.

We rely on a set of core architecture judgments, summarized in @tbl-architect-technical-judgments, to transform isolated results from models, tools, and domain specialists into a cohesive product recommendation. While we might distribute these individual judgments across different subsystems, properties, or design transitions, our architecture team must always step back and verify whether these fragmented domain claims assemble into one feasible system.

| **Judgment** | **Architectural question** | **Lighthouse consequence** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Problem choice and reframing** | Is the stated problem still the one our product needs solved? | Our task is not merely to maximize array utilization. We must decide whether an implementation-facing compute and software interface meets our mobile XR obligation. |
| **Abstraction** | Which details can we simplify for this decision, and which must remain visible? | A cycle-level array model can compare mappings locally, but it cannot hide compiler behavior, memory traffic, physical timing, or our 3\ W subsystem boundary from a freeze decision. |
| **System boundary** | Where do workload, software, hardware, package, physical design, and product effects meet in our architecture? | We cannot separate array dimensions and dataflow from the runtime, interconnect, memory, energy, and implementation path they require. |
| **Architecture synthesis** | Do our mechanisms, interfaces, software paths, implementation choices, and containment provisions form one feasible system? | Our array, compiler and runtime interface, memory path, 3\ W constraint, and fallback behavior must form one implementable subsystem rather than separate local wins. |
| **Missing constraints** | What has our formulation, representation, objective, or tool path left out? | Representative workloads, interface cost, subsystem power, implementation feasibility, reliability and security properties, and containment remain open obligations for us. |
| **Cross-layer tradeoff** | Which feasible point best serves our product when objectives conflict? | We must intentionally compose performance, energy, programmability, reversibility, schedule, and review burden rather than delegating them to separate optimizers. |
| **Mechanism and consequence** | Does our proposed explanation fit the observations, and what happens to our system if it is wrong? | Our failed directional shape-and-mapping explanation cannot support transfer. A wrong freeze could harden a poor software contract and saddle us with costly RTL and physical rework. |
| **Commitment under uncertainty** | Are our remaining risks understood, containable, and worth accepting given our available organizational capacity? | Our missing implementation-facing tests block the current freeze. The absent matched comparison independently leaves our AI program test unresolved. |

: **Architecture judgment gives technical work its system meaning.** As architects, we choose the question, abstraction, boundary, and consequence before our commitment authority decides whether the design advances.
{#tbl-architect-technical-judgments tbl-colwidths="[20,38,42]"}

Ultimately, any claim that we have a feasible system rests on our problem choice, abstractions, and system boundaries. Once we establish those foundations, architecture synthesis allows us to expose missing constraints and cross-layer tradeoffs that isolated specialist results simply cannot resolve. Our explanation of the underlying mechanisms, coupled with a clear-eyed view of remaining risks, then determines whether our recommendation warrants a firm commitment. In the Lighthouse project, working through these judgments is exactly how we create and synthesize the architecture – we are driving the design, not just rubber-stamping it after the fact.

Every one of these judgments relies fundamentally on the abstractions, components, and constraints we define. Together, they dictate exactly what a local result means for the success of our entire system.
## Choosing Abstractions, Components, and Constraints

An abstraction represents our deliberate technical choice about which details to expose for a given decision and which to simplify away. We might represent the same design candidate as an instruction mix, a dataflow graph, a cycle-level model, synthesizable RTL, a floorplan, or even a thermal model. None of these models constitute the architecture in isolation.[^fn-architecture-description-c11] Instead, because each representation highlights specific relationships while suppressing others, we must choose the model whose omissions are safe for the particular design action we have under review.

[^fn-architecture-description-c11]: **Architecture description**: ISO/IEC/IEEE 42010 distinguishes an entity's architecture from an architecture description that expresses it. The standard also specifies requirements for architecture viewpoints and model kinds, but it does not prescribe our chapter's organization, our specific design process, or our assignment of authority [@ISOIECIEEE2022ArchitectureDescription].

Our choice of abstraction directly dictates which components can meaningfully contribute to a design decision. As architects, we must ask what architectural state each predictor, generator, optimizer, conventional method, or tool is allowed to modify, and which independent observations constrain those changes. Simply piling on more components does not guarantee a better composed system. In fact, if a component's internal simplifications obscure a critical blocking property, the final result becomes far less trustworthy, even if that component boasts impressive local optimizations.

We can see this component-versus-system contrast clearly in the AlphaChip macro-placement case developed earlier in @sec-feedback-verification-trust. While the original paper emphasizes the component's impressive macro-placement capability [@MirhoseiniEtAl2021GraphPlacement], that section also documents the subsequent debates regarding how well those results generalize across different tool flows, baselines, and design data, as well as the inherent limits of using favorable proxies for placement quality. For our purposes, the architectural takeaway is much narrower. We, as architects, still define the block boundaries, curate the macro set, establish the timing and power constraints, determine the comparison basis, and run the routability and signoff checks. Ultimately, we must decide whether a given placement actually serves the chip's overarching goals. A highly capable component can certainly execute substantive design work, but it never owns the larger technical decision.

Beyond selecting individual components, we also architect how these pieces interact. We decide exactly which architectural state crosses an interface, which downstream component has the authority to revise that state, which independent checks can halt progress, and whether two seemingly distinct verification steps are secretly sharing the same flawed assumptions. The way we arrange this workflow fundamentally alters which design candidates we can propose, which critical properties we can observe, and, most importantly, which catastrophic errors might survive our gauntlet.

Often, our most consequential constraints first emerge as expert judgment rather than explicitly represented design state. As we discussed in @sec-architecture-20-ontology, this is *tacit knowledge* – the practical, hard-won insights that practitioners rely on but cannot always formalize completely [@Polanyi1966TacitDimension, p. 4]. For instance, our compiler specialist might intuitively know that a proposed new instruction will lack an efficient lowering path in our supported toolchain. Similarly, our physical design lead might immediately recognize that a specific placement heuristic is completely unsafe for our chosen power-grid geometry and current profile.

One promising application for AI assistance is helping us locate, compare, and organize these scattered expert judgments for formal review. However, simply writing down tacit knowledge does not magically render it authoritative. Any consequential architectural constraint, assumption, or claim requires a rigorous check commensurate with its risk and scope. We might delegate that check to a qualified automated method, a conventional EDA tool, a domain specialist, or an independent peer reviewer. While the domain specialist qualifies the meaning and boundaries of the rule, we – the architecture team – must separately decide whether it truly belongs in the permanent project record. If we accept it, we rigorously document its source, its precise scope, the interfaces it affects, any known conflicts, its expiration date, and the specific conditions that would prompt us to reopen the decision.

Consider a scenario where our physical designer enforces a rule against placing two high-current macros on the exact same power stripe. The physical-design specialist provides the qualifying geometry, the current basis, and the safe operating threshold. As architects, we then decide how to enforce this: do we encode this knowledge as explicit model state, formulate it as a hard environment constraint, deploy it as a downstream rejection check, or simply leave it as a scoped specialist judgment? We must also evaluate whether the resulting routing overhead still serves the larger design goals. Crucially, if we later change our power-grid template, we invalidate the original basis of the rule. We must then trigger another formal review, rather than blindly leaving the obsolete constraint in force as if it were timeless expertise.

We must remember that not every expert intuition should crystallize into a formal rule. While an unrecorded constraint risks being dangerously optimized away by our tools, an overgeneralized constraint can blindly reject highly innovative, valid designs. Our distinctive architectural responsibility is navigating this tension – deciding precisely whether a given piece of knowledge belongs in model state, an environment constraint, a rejection check, or human specialist judgment.

Ultimately, we must compose all of these resulting components, tools, and specialist judgments into a single, coherent, and highly effective architectural system.
## Integrating Across Layers and Disciplines

We only elevate a design candidate to a true architecture when its mechanisms and interfaces seamlessly interoperate across every layer governing product behavior. For our Lighthouse project, this means rigorously connecting the XR workload and algorithms down through the compiler and runtime, our instruction set architecture (ISA), microarchitecture, memory hierarchy and interconnects, RTL, physical design, and packaging. We also have to bind these elements against power and thermal limits, verification demands, and our user-facing product obligations. While a local optimization might offer compelling research value – even if another layer cannot yet implement it – we recognize that isolated improvements do not establish a usable, synthesized system result.

When we deploy design space search, we can identify useful candidates and effectively approximate the Pareto frontier introduced in @tbl-moonshot-decomposition – those feasible objective outcomes not dominated by any other viable design. However, actually selecting a point on that frontier remains a fundamentally different, deeply architectural act. For instance, we might widen a network link to improve our camera-ingest latency, but we must simultaneously absorb the cost of increased switching activity and routing pressure. Conversely, narrowing that link might save dynamic power while drastically increasing our queueing delays or software scheduling sensitivity. Sometimes, our designs can push out both objectives simultaneously before we ever hit a hard tradeoff. As architects, we do not simply assume conflict in advance; rather, we weigh the objectives, constraints, operating conditions, and overarching product consequences to determine exactly why one feasible point is ultimately preferable to another.

Once we map out these feasible points, our role as the architect is to recommend the specific configuration that best serves the product vision. Our commitment authority then crystallizes that recommendation into a binding product trajectory by authorizing a consequential design transition. To do this properly, our recommendation must encompass crucial system effects that no single automated optimizer could possibly represent: software turnover, difficult-to-reverse interfaces, verification capacity, rigid package constraints, deployment containment strategies, or strict user-experience thresholds. While a heavily weighted objective function can neatly encode a declared tradeoff, it can never tell us whether those mathematical weights still truly reflect the product we are trying to build.

We must remember that our architecture team composes specialist judgments; we do not replace them. Our compiler, verification, physical-design, and product domain experts each establish vital, specialized results within their own scopes. As architects, our synthesis task is to determine whether these disparate results actually align to form one coherent system decision, and we must constantly hunt for any unexamined interfaces hiding between them.

We can make this synthesis concrete by walking through a hypothetical future revision of the Lighthouse. Suppose our trace analysis supports the frame-rate target, our compiler search finds a legal tiling strategy, our RTL simulation decisively passes, our SRAM model satisfies its local bandwidth checks, and our accelerator block finally closes timing. Excellent – until we combine the results. Suddenly, we discover that our tiling raises burst traffic, the wider interface and added buffering push the subsystem beyond our strict 3\ W thermal limit, and a critical tail-latency case lacks any software fallback. To synthesize a working solution, we must change the system holistically: we assign tail handling directly to the CPU, narrow the accelerator interface, revise our buffering and scheduling schemes, and manually inject a fallback path. Our domain specialists then jump back in to reassess all affected contracts. While no such drastic revision was executed in the retained Lighthouse records, this sequence vividly illustrates the heart of architecture creation. We continually iterate on mechanisms, interfaces, and partitioning until our local, specialized results finally converge into one feasible, unified product.

Crucially, our team must relentlessly preserve this architectural coherence as work naturally disperses among various people, models, and tools. Candidate identity, baseline assumptions, strict interfaces, localized checks, and stopping conditions absolutely cannot disappear as we move between components. As architects, we thread these outputs together – from high-level workload behavior down through tiling, interconnect traffic, buffering, the rigid 3\ W boundary, and the software fallback mechanisms. We then produce a single, actionable recommendation bounded by an explicit scope, openly detailing both supporting and conflicting results, alongside all known limits. Ultimately, while our domain-level checks rigorously qualify what our recommendation can support, they do not – and cannot – authorize the final product commitment.
## Interpreting Results and Disagreement

As we established in @sec-feedback-verification-trust, a check can only support what its scope, uncertainty, and independence justify. However, computer architecture introduces another layer of complexity when qualified results actively disagree. For instance, a performance result might support a local ranking, yet if we cannot explain the underlying mechanism, we cannot safely transfer that result to a changed workload, software path, interface, or implementation. When faced with this, we must either narrow our claim, request a discriminating test, or keep the dependent transition firmly blocked.

We cannot settle these decisions simply by counting votes. First, our domain experts must determine whether the conflicting checks actually encode the same contract and conditions. If they do, a blocking failure remains a failure. If they do not, we must correct the architectural abstraction or interface definition, then rerun the affected paths. When our experts cannot reconcile these scopes, we must keep the transition blocked and escalate the unresolved system contract – resisting the urge to just choose the more convenient result.

Consider a coherence verifier that returns a counterexample against a declared blocking property, even though our software model treats that exact same execution as legal. We cannot simply weaken the property, discard the failing workload, or creatively recast the counterexample as a pass. Instead, our first technical question must be whether the property and the software model encode the identical product contract. If they do, the candidate fails. If they do not, we must correct the underlying architecture problem and rerun both paths. Ultimately, this kind of disagreement exposes a fundamental system-interface error that no localized score can resolve.

Of course, not every uncertainty halts all progress. Suppose we have two feasible candidates with overlapping estimates for tail latency and subsystem power. As architects, we must identify whether workload sampling, model error, or an untested operating corner could reverse our choice. We then request the least costly higher-fidelity observation capable of discriminating between them – such as matched cycle-level runs or implementation-facing power analysis. If no available observation can resolve the overlap within our budget, we must keep our recommendation narrow and our choice reversible, rather than carelessly treating the nominal mean as a decisive mandate.

Ultimately, our interpretation connects each result to a concrete consequence. A timing pass at one corner cannot magically handwave an open power-delivery failure, just as proving a declared property cannot guarantee that the property accurately captured the desired product behavior. We must synthesize and integrate these tightly scoped judgments to form a coherent architectural vision.

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Architecture judgment does not begin where automation ends"}
While automation may handle local formulation, exploration, implementation, and analysis, our architectural judgment dictates the problem, the abstraction, and the system boundaries. We must synthesize cross-layer dependencies, interpret conflicting evidence, and forge a supported recommendation. Every design review must identify the ultimate decision-maker and trace exactly how isolated results unite to form one feasible system. Without this rigorous oversight, even perfectly successful tool runs can prop up a fundamentally flawed architecture.
:::

Any real design commitment demands this fully integrated account of our architecture problem, the system we are building, and the true meaning of our results.
## Architecture Result, Program Claim, and Commitment

When we synthesize our technical findings, we produce a comprehensive architecture recommendation, rather than a final commitment. In our recommendation, we outline the preferred design alongside credible alternatives, detail the specific conditions and structural checks underpinning our comparisons, and highlight any conflicting data or gaps in evidence. We must also explicitly set the limits that will govern our next design transition. Crucially, while we integrate findings into a unified, cross-layer architectural recommendation, we do not override our specialized peers. Our domain experts in verification, timing, physical design, power integrity, safety, security, and reliability retain full responsibility for their respective signoffs and results.

Our two independent evaluation tests from @sec-moonshot remain perfectly intact. We rely on rigorous architectural evidence to establish exactly what our design can support when subjected to required workload, software, implementation, physical, and verification checks. Concurrently, as we explored in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, we separately classify our program claims as supported, unsupported, or unresolved by comparing holistic design methodologies. We must remember that this status reflects whether we should adopt a specific approach, not whether we commit to a particular architecture. Ultimately, neither of these tests gives us the authority to force a design transition.

Once we have a concrete result in hand, our responsible domain specialists clearly state its validity and scope. As architects, we then weave that validated result into our cross-layer technical recommendation, synthesizing it with other qualified evidence. From there, our designated commitment authority decides whether we advance the design, freeze an interface, push into implementation, proceed to tape-out, or authorize a release. The organization accountable for these steps must resource the work, own all product consequences, and maintain the operational agility to monitor and even reopen the decision if necessary. While a single individual might wear several of these hats, we must recognize that generating a qualified result, formulating a system recommendation, and executing an authorized decision remain fundamentally distinct architectural actions.

We often draw upon the same underlying study records to inform these judgments, yet each judgment answers a distinctly different question in our design process. For instance, achieving a favorable architecture result does not automatically prove we made a meaningful AI contribution, just as securing a supported program claim does not give us the green light for a design transition. Similarly, if we refuse a specific design, that action alone does not invalidate our broader program claim. We must be strict: no single result can supply the missing architectural evidence required for an entirely separate judgment.

The program claim statuses we developed in @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect deliberately leave various architectural pathways open. Consequently, no single status can unilaterally dictate our final design commitment (@tbl-two-closing-decisions).

| **Program claim status** | **What it means for architecture commitment** |
|  –  |  –  |
| **Supported** | Our repeated, matched comparisons across declared tasks and conditions show that our complete AI-assisted approach clears the relevant architecture-quality or total-cost decision boundary. We may still refuse the architecture if we find the physical design, supporting evidence, organizational capacity, or residual risk to be unacceptable. |
| **Unsupported** | Our matched comparisons, having sufficient coverage and resolving power, demonstrate that our claimed advantage either fails to clear our core decision criterion or directly contradicts the claim. Nevertheless, we may still commit to a structurally sound architecture if it is backed by solid evidence produced through conventional or human-directed design methodologies. |
| **Unresolved** | We find the comparison to be missing, incomplete, or severely underpowered, and its high uncertainty prevents us from determining if we cleared the architectural decision boundary. We cannot justify an adoption claim. We may only proceed with the architecture if independent design evidence explicitly supports it; otherwise, it must remain uncommitted while we complete the missing verification work. |

: **Program claim status and architecture commitment remain independent.** We cannot substitute a favorable result on one for a favorable result on the other in our architectural methodologies. {#tbl-two-closing-decisions tbl-colwidths="[22,78]"}

Our two evaluation tests can readily diverge in either direction. Consequently, the evidence we gather for adopting a novel program or synthesis workflow cannot, on its own, settle whether we should commit to a particular hardware architecture. The critical remaining question for us is determining exactly what type of architectural commitment might follow, and precisely who within our engineering organization owns it.
## Making and Limiting a Design Commitment

When we make an architecture commitment, we make a fundamental technical system choice. We are selecting a specific design and its interfaces for further implementation, product integration, or release under stated conditions. In our synthesis, we treat reversibility as a first-class design variable. Early in exploration, a commitment remains cheap to revise. However, that flexibility vanishes once our choice hardens into an instruction set architecture (ISA), a fixed software interface, a physical floorplan, a package, or a final mask set. Our proposed decision rule is straightforward: we must raise the evidence burden systematically as our design reversals become more costly and consequential.

Our commitment explicitly states what design advances, which alternatives we rejected, which conditions our evidence covered, what uncertainty remains, and exactly what would invalidate our choice. We are not certifying that the design is perfect. Instead, we establish that our selected system is strictly preferable to credible alternatives for our stated product obligation, and that we have bounded the remaining uncertainty well enough to justify the next architectural transition.

We must keep three critical technical decisions strictly separate. Simply running design work does not establish what a given result actually supports, and merely establishing that support does not automatically commit our architecture (@tbl-lighthouse-action-rights).

| **Decision** | **Technical question** | **Boundary** |
|  –  |  –  |  –  |
| **Execute design work** | What candidate state may this person, model, or tool change, and when must it stop? | Our work stays strictly within the declared design space, interfaces, budget, and evaluator boundary. Execution cannot silently change a requirement or acceptance condition. |
| **Establish what a result supports** | What does this check show about this artifact under these conditions and assumptions? | Our relevant domain specialists own the result's validity and domain scope; the architect determines how that qualified result applies to our overarching system decision. A waiver or later judgment cannot simply relabel a failed or inconclusive check. |
| **Commit the architecture** | Does the integrated design justify the next consequential transition? | Our architecture decision carefully composes alternatives, cross-layer results, specialist concurrences, uncertainty, containment, and residual risk without ever replacing our strict domain signoff. |

: **Execution, support, and commitment remain distinctly separate technical decisions in our methodology.** We separating them, we prevent a successful tool run or a favorable local result from silently authorizing our architecture. {#tbl-lighthouse-action-rights tbl-colwidths="[22,38,40]"}

While a classic human-automation framework separates information acquisition, analysis, decision selection, and action implementation to ask how much of each function we should automate [@ParasuramanEtAl2000LevelsAutomation], it only provides a useful precedent. It demonstrates the value of separating functions before assigning automation, but it does not fully prescribe our specific distinction among executing design work, establishing evidentiary support, and formally committing an architecture.

We cannot let a later judgment rewrite the recorded result of a completed check. Our architecture team can certainly add new results, and changed conditions can render an earlier result inapplicable to our current candidate, but the original outcome remains immutable.

Even though the organizational assignment of these decisions differs across teams, we must never collapse their distinct technical meanings. For example, an AI-assisted system might perform reversible actions and trigger our declared stops, while our domain specialists establish exactly what those automated results support. Ultimately, the architect integrates those findings, and our commitment authority decides whether the overarching system advances.

### Stating Residual Risk

Committing to an architecture does not mean we have magically erased every uncertainty. Rather, it means we understand the remaining failure modes well enough to accept, mitigate, or block them. When we grant a bounded exception, we do not change the underlying test result, and a mandatory requirement remains fully blocking unless we deliberately alter the requirement itself. We treat residual risk as an inherent technical property of our decision, not as an administrative label pasted on after the design advances.

Our residual-risk statement is only usable if a reviewer can explicitly connect the failure mode to its consequence, its remaining uncertainty, the detecting check, and our containment or rollback action. We propose these five items as the absolute minimum. If we lack a reliable check, operating restriction, or containment path to detect or limit the failure, we must block the design transition entirely.

To test what containment practically requires, consider a hypothetical future Lighthouse candidate featuring an optional vector-turbo mode whose subsystem power and thermal behavior remain insufficiently characterized. This mode is not part of our retained Lighthouse evidence. Merely retaining its circuitry for later study would never justify actually enabling it. For us to craft a defensible exception, we would require a rigorously verified disabled state, an enable path strictly restricted to an authorized lab or privileged service mode, and fully verified reset, fault, and access-control behavior. We would also demand proof that the disabled circuitry does not violate our base design's functional, timing, power, or security requirements, alongside a named owner and a firm expiration tied to post-silicon characterization. If we cannot validate the disabled state, isolation, or restricted enable path, we must remove the feature or halt the design's advance. The exception does not magically transform missing evidence into a passing grade. At expiration, we face a strict decision point: we must authorize enablement using new evidence, renew a narrower exception, keep the mode permanently disabled, or physically remove it.

If we allow repeated exceptions, a known failure rapidly morphs into our accepted baseline, triggering the normalization of deviance brilliantly described by Vaughan [@Vaughan1996Challenger]. We enforcing expiration and reopening, we prevent a temporary decision from becoming permanent merely because our reporting systems fall silent. We borrow this concept to address the repeated acceptance of engineering exceptions; we are not trying to equate our chip review processes with Challenger's life-and-death safety stakes or unique organizational context.

### Design Containment Before Commitment

Our containment authority truly matters only when our design provides a credible technical lever. Depending on the exact architectural failure, that lever might manifest as a verified feature-disable path, a safe firmware fallback, a thermal derating mode, a redundant physical resource, a strict isolation boundary, a rollback path, or simply our refusal to expose the capability to software. However, we must recognize that some failures offer no safe containment short of physical repair or outright replacement. If we lack a credible containment lever, that absence alone provides ample reason for us to refuse a difficult-to-reverse commitment.

We must remember that disable mechanisms are not universal insurance policies. We still have to verify the disabled state, completely isolate the failure from required behavior, and ensure our control path remains highly available even under the active fault being contained. While errata and later silicon steppings give us established channels for describing and repairing some post-silicon defects, we know from experience that not every erratum has a viable workaround, and not every subsequent stepping actually fixes the problem.[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]

[^fn-errata-stepping-c11]: **Errata and silicon steppings**: An erratum records a design defect or error that may cause released silicon to deviate from our published specifications. A silicon stepping identifies a particular hardware revision. For example, Intel's specification update lists numerous errata for its B2 stepping with the status `No Fix`, illustrating to us that documenting a defect does not guarantee we plan to repair it [@Intel2014CoreMIOUpdate].

### The Pending Lighthouse Commitment

Our current lack of system-boundary and implementation evidence strongly supports a technical recommendation to keep our Lighthouse transition open. This missing data does not prove that our design passes or fails, and it certainly does not authorize a final architecture commitment.

::: {.callout-lighthouse title="The Lighthouse commitment remains open"}
Our prospective cache study did not run, and our separate local array result completely fails to establish the full workload and software interface, the 3\ W subsystem boundary, or the pinned physical implementation. Consequently, our architect's present technical recommendation is to leave the freeze and commitment undecided, pending fully qualified checks of those missing requirements. We emphasize that this is a recommendation to continue our technical work; it is neither a finding that the design passes or fails, nor permission to advance the pipeline. We keep these two records strictly separate for our later review.
:::

We must ensure that a later review qualifies those missing results before our architect can safely recommend advancing the design, and well before our commitment authority can ever authorize that transition. If we wish to make a broader program adoption claim, we must separately demand repeated, meticulously matched comparisons of our complete architectural approaches.
## Responsibility Continues Through Challenge and Reopening

We must retain the ability to challenge and reopen our own architectural decisions. Simply naming an owner does not automatically build this capacity. To truly maintain control over a design, we have to ensure that our design candidates, boundary conditions, rejected alternatives, simulation results, unresolved disagreements, and overall status remain fully inspectable. Our architecture teams and domain specialists alike need unhindered access to the tools, testbenches, and artifacts capable of exposing a mistake later in the lifecycle.

### Maintaining the Capacity to Challenge

Bainbridge's irony of automation warns us that heavy automation can gradually erode the hands-on practice that developed our technical intuition in the first place [@Bainbridge1983Ironies]. We are not arguing to keep routine verification manual, but we do need to actively test whether our architects and specialists can still critically inspect tool behavior, analyze failed candidates, and formulate cross-layer diagnoses when the automation inevitably falls short.

Elish coined the term *moral crumple zone* to describe a person forced to absorb the blame for an automated system despite lacking meaningful control over its behavior [@Elish2019MoralCrumpleZones]. Naming a reviewer who lacks both access to decisive artifacts and the authority to halt a design transition creates an analogous risk in our architecture workflows. Even with access, we face *automation bias* – the tendency to blindly accept incorrect automated synthesis advice or overlook layout problems our tools failed to flag. Skitka et al. documented both of these errors in a simulated flight task aided by imperfect automation [@SkitkaEtAl1999AutomationBias]. While flying a simulator isn't direct evidence of how we review chip architectures, these lessons powerfully motivate us to rigorously test whether our proposed challenge paths actually work under pressure.

We must demonstrate this challenge capacity through concrete technical work. An architect or domain specialist needs the ability to reproduce or commission selective, decisive checks. We must be able to inspect failed design candidates, diagnose intentionally seeded logic faults, and reassess our evidence whenever an underlying tool or architectural parameter changes. For at least a few exercises, we should require an independent human diagnosis before we even look at the automated tool's recommendation. Each of these exercises concludes with our architects recording how their findings alter the baseline recommendation, leaving the commitment authority to decide whether the design transition advances, narrows, holds, or fully reopens. This approach directly connects our technical competence to the architectural decisions we are challenging, elevating the process beyond generic workforce training.

Opaque external dependencies do not magically absolve us of responsibility. A black-box vendor model, a licensed IP block, a foundry process design kit (PDK), or a commercial EDA tool may restrict what our architecture teams can directly inspect. When making a commitment, we must rigorously identify the exact IP versions, interface assumptions, available independent cross-checks, and the specific failure modes that will remain difficult to diagnose. If our observations cannot confidently support the required claim or provide a safe fallback mechanism, moving forward is fundamentally unsound. We must remember that a vendor certificate merely establishes provenance; it is never a substitute for an independent technical check.

### Transferring the Technical Basis

Our unresolved Lighthouse project makes this ongoing responsibility highly concrete. When we hand off that project, the receiving architects need more than just a final status update; they require the complete technical foundation and the specific conditions that could eventually support a later decision. Any transfer of architectural responsibility must therefore pass along the deep technical basis, not merely a high-level summary report.

When we defer work, we carry forward the missing obligations that previously prevented a commitment. Similarly, a rejected microarchitectural alternative must retain the explicit basis for its rejection, returning to consideration only if a relevant physical or workload condition fundamentally changes.

The successor team must receive the exact candidate release identity, the well-defined design question, and the specific system boundaries. We have to provide them with our baseline assumptions, explored alternatives, and the complete spectrum of decisive results – passed, failed, inconclusive, and notably missing. Furthermore, we must clearly outline the remaining uncertainty and detail any validated containment paths. A successful transfer explicitly identifies which shifts in workload, software stack, EDA tools, manufacturing process, interface standards, or observed behaviors would render the original decision entirely inapplicable. If proprietary boundaries limit reproduction, the transfer documentation must clearly specify which artifacts only a heavily credentialed domain specialist can inspect.

Whenever one of those critical conditions changes, our architects must initiate a technical reconsideration. We do not expect the new team to personally rerun every historical regression check. Instead, they ensure the relevant domain specialists thoughtfully reconsider the decision, preventing us from blindly reusing an outdated result just because a report happens to be sitting on a server. We explore this transfer analysis deeply in @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, addressing exactly what artifacts transfer cleanly and which dependent verification work we must aggressively repeat.

### Monitoring and Reopening the Decision

The technical basis we transfer dictates exactly what our monitoring systems must watch. We identify which workload mixes, software and firmware stacks, operating voltage ranges, supplier component versions, tool qualifications, and physical thermal conditions demand continuous observation. Product telemetry gives us incredible visibility, exposing architectural shifts through tail latency spikes, power and thermal excursions, corrected and uncorrected ECC errors, link degradation, and recurring reset signatures. However, these observations only matter if we tie them directly to a boundary condition or a failure mode capable of overturning an established architecture decision.

Any reopening trigger must immediately drive a named technical action. A shifting workload or a major software release might force us to requalify our performance and memory hierarchy behavior. When we encounter a new erratum, a supplier revision, or a production failure in deployed systems, we may need to execute a containment action, push a firmware patch, derate the operating frequency, disable a faulty feature, tape out a new stepping, or even refuse further deployment. Our specialists pinpoint the affected results, our architects revise the cross-layer recommendation, and our commitment authority dictates the next transition. Ultimately, our accountable organization owns the product response. In this light, system monitoring isn't just a generic exercise in operating a learned model; it is the active maintenance of our living architecture decisions.

Observed failures frequently force us to reopen a commitment. While failing silicon clearly proves that a breakdown occurred under specific observed conditions, it rarely hands us the root cause. Our subsequent technical investigations must still rigorously disentangle whether the fault stems from the workload, the software stack, the core hardware logic, the packaging, manufacturing variations, environmental stressors, or operational edge cases.

The infamous Pentium FDIV bug, discussed in @sec-stronger-evaluation-expensive, perfectly illustrates this reality. Edelman documents five specific lookup-table entries that should have returned a 2 but instead returned a 0 [@Edelman1997PentiumDivision, p. 57]. While this catastrophic defect escaped into released silicon, the public account does not reconstruct every internal handoff that allowed the error to slip through. Its role for us here is much narrower but deeply instructive: evidence from systems deployed in the wild completely invalidated the confidence behind a released processor design. It demanded immediate, renewed architecture work, aggressive containment strategies, and a hard decision about how to handle the affected products.
## Common Pitfalls

As we shift our methodologies toward AI-assisted architecture, we inherently introduce new risks when delegating complex technical work. While automation can massively accelerate design space exploration and rigorous verification, it fundamentally cannot absorb our accountability for cross-layer synthesis or the ultimate product consequences. The following pitfalls illustrate common failures we must navigate to maintain true architectural ownership.

**Conflating Execution with Authority.** We frequently fall into the trap of assuming that because an automated agent can execute a complex tool flow or propose a novel design, it holds the authority to commit that design. However, execution always remains within a bounded evaluator. Our role in commitment requires us to synthesize intricate cross-layer tradeoffs and shoulder the residual risk. We must never let a seemingly successful tool run silently authorize a fundamental architecture transition without our explicit, expert review.

**Relying Solely on Opaque Signoffs.** When integrating third-party vendor models, licensed IP blocks, or complex AI-generated subsystems, our teams sometimes accept a generic "pass" without interrogating the underlying interface assumptions. If we cannot trace a critical failure through an opaque component, or if we lack the independent checks required to validate its integration, we have surrendered our vital technical contact. Without that deep understanding, we simply cannot defend the coherence of our system design.

**Normalization of Deviance in AI Assistance.** A highly capable AI system might propose clever workarounds or exceptions to bypass local constraints – such as disabling a failing feature or stretching a delicate thermal limit. If we repeatedly accept these exceptions without enforcing rigorous containment paths, strict expiration conditions, and robust post-silicon validation, our project inevitably normalizes deviance. We have to treat every single accepted workaround as a temporary technical debt, never as our new architectural baseline.
## Open Questions

As automated synthesis tools absorb the repetitive mechanics of design generation and verification, our intellectual focus must shift. We are no longer just accelerating execution; we must now rigorously compose, interrogate, and govern the complex systems we build. The open questions we outline below go far beyond transient operational hurdles. They expose foundational gaps in our ability to maintain technical contact, assign authority, and bound uncertainty whenever autonomous agents drive consequential microarchitectural and system-level transitions. Resolving these challenges demands our rigorous academic inquiry – whether we tackle them through focused architecture papers or deep doctoral research. Rather than dictating a rigid research agenda, we offer these questions to mark critical, unresolved computer architecture challenges. We must continually ask what AI-assisted methodologies make possible, and what core architectural judgment we must preserve as our design workflows permanently change.

**Maintaining architectural judgment.** As we automate more localized, block-level design tasks, we – as researchers, practitioners, and students – must preserve our ability to frame high-level problems, integrate specialist results, and critically challenge plausible but flawed recommendations.

- **How can we determine whether we retain the technical capacity to challenge an AI-assisted recommendation?** True technical capacity extends far beyond simply having access to a formal checker. As architects, we must maintain enough independent system understanding to recognize exactly when a plausible cross-layer optimization should be reopened and scrutinized. We currently lack robust methods to detect the erosion of this critical capacity before it triggers a consequential silicon or system failure.

- **Which pedagogical and training interventions best preserve our capacity to challenge AI-driven synthesis systems?** Any credible evaluation of our training methods must measure our independent problem framing, our ability to detect unsupported cross-layer conclusions, and our diagnostic skill at catching seeded failures after we delegate routine design tasks. Identifying the interventions that successfully preserve our architectural intuition – and reveal its erosion prior to critical tape-out commitments – remains an open challenge for our community.

**Assigning authority and responsibility.** When we delegate technical work to intelligent tools, we still require explicit boundaries among our automated agents, domain specialists, lead architects, tape-out authorities, and the accountable organization.

- **How does dividing technical responsibility affect our ability to detect and veto an unsupported cross-layer decision?** How we assign tasks dictates who inspects decisive artifacts and who holds the final authority to halt a flawed design transition. As researchers and practitioners, we can use experiments with seeded interface contradictions to benchmark our detection rates, our access to decisive evidence, and our safe stopping mechanisms – without blindly assuming that a single organizational structure optimally fits every design team.

- **What diagnostic access and stopping authority must accompany our responsibility for AI-assisted architecture decisions?** We cannot hold a named reviewer accountable without giving them access to decisive evidence and the absolute authority to block an unsupported transition. We face an unresolved challenge in determining exactly what level of access and authority proves sufficient across varying design stakes, ensuring tight accountability without bottlenecking every technical judgment through a centralized approval loop.

**Preserving visibility across system boundaries.** Highly capable AI assistance successfully expands the work our architecture teams delegate only if unfamiliar failures remain traceable across abstraction layers and deeply opaque generated components.

- **What technical visibility must we retain to diagnose an unfamiliar cross-layer failure?** Truly useful visibility must seamlessly connect a symptom in one architectural layer to its root cause or consequence in another, without overwhelming us with every intermediate generated artifact. We face an ongoing challenge in deciding precisely which structural relationships must remain transparent and inspectable as our synthesis tools and generated IP blocks continually evolve.

- **Which observable interface properties allow us to expose consequential failures within opaque supplier IP or tool components?** Opaque hardware blocks need not reveal their proprietary internals, but their interfaces must expose enough behavioral state for us to detect consequential violations before they propagate deep into the rest of the system. For our community of researchers and practitioners, it remains an open question which interface properties optimally balance necessary design abstraction with essential diagnostic visibility.

As our architectural practice matures alongside these tools, we must purposefully decide what new capabilities to build – and exactly what human judgment, authority, education, interfaces, and diagnostic access we must fiercely preserve.
## Closing the Moonshot

::: {.callout-design-principle title="Delegate technical work, not architectural accountability"}
While we can fully delegate technical execution, a named, technically qualified, and institutionally empowered authority must retain the absolute power to stop, commit, or reopen any architecture decision. Our accountable organization must own the downstream consequences and provide the necessary resources for monitoring and recovery. As commitment authorities, we must directly inspect the technical basis, maintaining a strict separation between a recommendation and a final commitment. We consider a review to have failed this principle if the assigned owner cannot inspect decisive evidence, block a transition, or secure resources to respond to post-commitment failures.
:::

We close this book without a definitive Lighthouse verdict. As we recorded in @sec-running-the-loop, our prospective cache study did not run. Furthermore, the separately executed array study supports only a localized no-change finding for the specific array shapes we evaluated. It supplies zero evidence for the full system, our 3\ W subsystem target, or the pinned physical implementation. Consequently, we recorded no final architecture commitment.

Providing these missing checks and matched comparisons is exactly the work we are asking the machine-learning and computer-architecture communities to take up. To build a credible architectural benchmark, we require a versioned workload, software stack, and reference design. We must define a clear action space and constraints; deliver executable tool and evidence tracks; and establish evaluator-owned checks and metrics. Crucially, we need matched conventional and no-added-assistance baselines backed by total-cost accounting. We also demand retained provenance, rigorous contamination controls, clear task splits, and durable governance for maintenance and versioning. The XR Lighthouse Request supplies our core design question and outlines these exact requirements. Ultimately, building the versioned artifacts, executable tracks, and governance structures to realize this benchmark is the grand challenge we present – because today, none of it exists.

We taking up this challenge, we preserve our two independent tests. First, our matched comparisons must conclusively establish whether the complete AI-assisted system actually improves architecture capability, lowers total cost, or both, when compared to a credible alternative within its assessed envelope. Even if we can support that program claim, we – as architects – must separately integrate the technical evidence and recommend whether the selected design and its residual risks truly justify commitment. A named commitment authority must then make the final call on whether the architecture advances. If our assessment finds no clear adoption advantage, we might still advance the same architecture through a conventional workflow. We must also recognize that a component-level or narrower AI contribution remains fundamentally unresolved when controlled replacement or ablation cannot isolate it from broader system interactions. We cannot let the absence of a verdict masquerade as a success claim.

Our discipline now urgently needs durable cross-layer abstractions that directly connect workload and software behavior down to the microarchitecture and physical implementation. We require interfaces that explicitly expose assumptions and uncertainty to our tools and reviewers, alongside holistic evaluations that compare complete architectural approaches rather than isolated model outputs. Moreover, we must fundamentally rethink our training: we need to prepare architects to engineer not just the computer system itself, but the entire AI-assisted design environment used to study it.

Architecture 2.0 asks us to boldly engineer and leverage AI-assisted design systems while fiercely owning the architecture problem, the cross-layer synthesis, the final technical recommendation, and its continued validity. While AI dramatically extends the scale of technical work we can attempt, it is ultimately up to us as architects to decide whether the resulting mechanisms and interfaces form a single, coherent system. We make the recommendation on what should be built, a named commitment authority decides whether the system advances, and our accountable organization remains answerable for the product's real-world consequences. Furthermore, we must be ready to reopen our technical recommendations the moment workloads, software, tools, process conditions, or observed silicon behaviors shift. It is this relentless, continuing technical oversight that elevates capable automation into true computer architecture.
